# The Crossing: A Plan for Moving from Licenses to Subscriptions

## The Plan on Two Pages

*(The plan itself, suitable for adoption. Everything that follows is the reasoning and the machinery.)*

**Our posture.** The subscription must be a magnet, not a mandate. Customers who feel pushed will push back; customers who feel courted will come. We will never end-of-life what we sold as perpetual — a deed is a deed. The trough is not the risk; the *surprise* is. So we name the trough before it arrives, give it a shape we chose, and walk the board, our largest investors, our senior salespeople, and our top hundred accounts across the bridge before asking any of them to stand on it. Nothing in this plan is announced before it is consulted.

**The offer.** Three subscription tiers built around continuous delivery rather than version numbers. A **perpetual parachute**: after three consecutive subscribed years, a departing customer keeps a perpetual license to the then-current version, with twelve months of security maintenance — costed, scoped, and accounted for, not merely promised. A **heritage line**: perpetual remains available at a premium for regulated and government buyers, behind eligibility gates, a bookings cap, and an annual sunset review — an escape valve that makes the main path feel chosen. **Dual-run rights** for twelve months during cutover.

**The migration.** A published, declining credit schedule — generous in year one, thinner in year two, standard in year three. Gravity, not a wall; the market sets its own deadline. Credits, never discounts: the list price holds; the welcome expires. Upgrade amnesty for customers on old versions. Three-year price locks for early movers. Cohorts sequenced: new logos first, then upgrade-due customers, then maintenance customers, then the lapsed. A customer council consulted at the design stage, so the announcement ratifies what their input shaped.

**The pricing.** Subscription list priced at parity with each customer's annualized historical spend — license amortized, plus upgrades, plus maintenance — so budgets continue uninterrupted. The chosen shape: GAAP revenue down roughly 8% in year one, a trough of 20–25% across years two and three, inflection in year four, prior peak crossed in year five. Billings trough only half as deep, because annual prepay and multi-year locks pull cash forward. We considered a deeper, faster crossing and a shallower, slower one; we chose the middle deliberately, and we publish the choice.

**The compensation.** Reps are paid on the company we are building: commission on first-year contract value at signing, a renewal trail for years two and three, clawback on twelve-month churn, and a premium rate on multi-year prepaid deals — so the comp plan itself pulls cash into the trough. Migration conversions earn 1.3x quota credit in year one, declining with the credit schedule. Heritage deals earn half credit at a reduced rate, behind deal-desk approval — the loophole is legal but economically unattractive. A twenty-four-month income bridge guarantees floors so our best people are not asked to fund the transition personally.

**The investor plan.** We pre-announce the trough with its chosen shape and commit to it. Two quarters before launch, the scoreboard pivots to ARR, net revenue retention, billings, deferred revenue, and conversion coverage — before the old metrics deteriorate. We teach the accounting plainly: the trough is partly optical, because licenses recognized upfront become subscriptions recognized ratably, and cash will outrun GAAP revenue throughout. The board approves the transition with milestones and tripwires attached, and pre-agrees the responses to each tripwire — so a triggered response is execution, not improvisation.

**The entitlement charter.** Nothing you bought is taken; everything you bought is honored. Security patches for current and prior versions for five years, with published dates. Owed upgrades delivered, or converted to credit at 1.5x. Twelve months' notice before any end of support. The new thing is simply better.

**The governance.** A transition council — finance, sales, product, customer council delegate, investor relations — meets monthly, owns the credit schedule and heritage approvals, and answers tripwires. Leaders who drift toward the old model are approached first quietly, by respected peers. The plan itself is reviewed annually; anything that no longer earns its place is retired.

---

## Opening Framing

Our competitor did not lose a fifth of its installed base because it chose subscriptions. It lost them because it chose *surprise and coercion*: an announcement instead of a conversation, a deadline instead of a slope, a mandate where a magnet was needed. The lesson is not that transitions fail. It is that transitions imposed *at* stakeholders fail — and transitions built *with* them, patiently and in the right order, endure.

This plan therefore proceeds on a quiet premise: every constituency that could break the crossing — customers who feel entitled, salespeople who feel threatened, investors who feel alarmed — is consulted before it is asked, and given a dignified path before it is given a deadline. The sections below supply the machinery.

---

## 1. Strategic Posture: Three Failure Modes, One Path Between Them

- **The cliff.** Ending perpetual abruptly and forcing migration. This is the competitor's path: a 20% installed-base loss, concentrated — as such losses always are — among the customers with the most options.
- **The drift.** Offering both models indefinitely with no gravitational pull. The two-model company carries duplicate engineering, duplicate support, duplicate messaging — and never escapes. The deepest trough is the one that never ends.
- **The revolt.** Converting the pricing model without converting the people paid on the old one. A sales force compensated on large upfront deals will sabotage subscription selling quietly and completely, and top performers will leave at the exact moment the trough demands their best.

The path between them: **subscription-only for new customers from day one, gravity-based migration for the installed base, a comp plan rebuilt before the pricing plan ships, and a trough named before it arrives.**

---

## 2. The Offer: Tiers, a Parachute, and a Heritage Line

**Three tiers, one idea.** Standard, Professional, Enterprise — differentiated by capability, support depth, and deployment options, all built on continuous delivery. Version numbers retire. The product improves every month; the subscription is how you already have it.

**The perpetual parachute — priced, not just promised.** After three consecutive subscribed years, a customer who leaves keeps a perpetual license to the then-current version. Stress-tested before it ships:

- *Cost model.* Expected redemption is bounded: customers who have paid three years have already absorbed the switching cost, and most who leave would leave anyway — the parachute converts a bitter exit into a soft one and keeps the door open for return. We model redemption at 5–8% of the subscribed base; the liability is reviewed quarterly by the council.
- *Scope limits.* The parachute freezes at the then-current version, carries twelve months of security maintenance, and then support ends — a perpetual license without maintenance decays gracefully, and we say so plainly rather than letting the promise hollow out. Continued maintenance-only contracts are available at a premium.
- *Churn incentive at year three.* Answered structurally: renewal pricing improves with tenure, and the version a customer would parachute out on is always eighteen months behind the one subscribers are using.
- *Accounting.* The parachute is likely a material right under ASC 606 — a separate performance obligation requiring a slice of subscription revenue (modeled at 5–8%) to be deferred until vesting or expiry. We model this with our auditors *before* announcement, so the promise never becomes a restatement.
- *Anti-gaming.* The parachute vests once per account. Returning customers re-enter at standard pricing, not amnesty pricing.

**The heritage line — with guardrails.** Perpetual remains available, because some buyers (government, defense, regulated industries) have procurement regimes that genuinely require it — and because the visible existence of a chosen alternative makes the main path feel chosen. Guardrails: written eligibility criteria and deal-desk approval; pricing at 2.5–3x annual subscription upfront plus 22–25% annual maintenance, so five-year cost of ownership clearly favors subscription; a bookings cap (no more than 15% of quarterly bookings in year one, 10% in year two, 5% in year three, with excess requiring CFO sign-off); reduced commission, per Section 5; and an annual sunset review by the council. The heritage line is a valve, not a business.

**Dual-run rights.** Twelve months of parallel operation during cutover, standard. No migration should be a leap.

---

## 3. The Migration: Gravity, Not a Wall

**The declining credit schedule — published, not negotiated.** Year one: migration credits up to 60% of first-year subscription value, sized to the customer's remaining upgrade entitlement and paid-up maintenance. Year two: up to 40%. Year three: standard pricing. The schedule is public, so no customer is humiliated by a deadline they learned too late, and no rep can invent a better deal in a hallway.

**Credits, never discounts.** The list price is forever; the welcome is temporary. Discounting the subscription itself would set a low anchor that every renewal would re-fight. Crediting money already spent honors the past without mortgaging the future.

**Sequencing — the quiet order matters:**

- *Wave 0 (from launch):* New logos are subscription-only. No one's entitlement is touched; the model proves itself on uncontested ground.
- *Wave 1:* Customers due for a paid upgrade within twelve months — already budgeting, already expecting change.
